comparisons.peer_topic: Regulatory VaR Back-Testing Definition and Basel III Requirements
comparisons.peer_summary: Citi performs regulatory VaR back-testing under Basel III by comparing the daily one-day VaR at a 99% confidence interval to buy-and-hold profit and loss, which excludes realized trading revenue, net interest, fees, commissions, intra-day P&L, and changes in reserves.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures address VaR back-testing as a core component of market risk management. While GS simply references the VaR table in this specific sentence, Citi elaborates on the regulatory requirement to perform back-testing under Basel III by comparing the daily one-day VaR at a 99% confidence interval to buy-and-hold profit and loss.

sentences.text: The table below presents our average daily VaR.
In accordance with Basel III, Citi is required to perform back-testing to evaluate the effectiveness of its Regulatory VaR model.

Regulatory VaR back-testing is the process in which the daily one-day VaR, at a 99% confidence interval, is compared to the buy-and-hold profit and loss (i.e., the profit and loss impact if the portfolio is held constant at the end of the day and re-priced the following day).

comparisons.peer_summary: The Firm performs daily VaR model backtesting by comparing Risk Management VaR with daily gains and losses. These gains and losses exclude specific revenue components such as fees, commissions, and net interest income, and are defined consistently with Basel III capital rules.
comparisons.comparison: Both GS and JPM discuss VaR in the context of risk metrics and back-testing. GS references a table of average daily VaR, whereas JPM details its daily VaR model backtesting process, which compares Risk Management VaR results with daily gains and losses consistent with Basel III capital rules.
